To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the number of short negative (arbitrary) counterexamples is a crucial factor in the learnability of languages; (2) the size of counterexamples is a key parameter; (3) the number of counterexamples is not the only parameter; (4) the size of positive examples also matters; and, (5) the number of positive examples can also be a crucial parameter.

(a) a single short counterexample can sometimes be better than any bounded number (including unbounded) of counterexamples of smallest length and (b) a bounded number of short counterexample can be better than an unbounded number of counterexamples.

(1) learners using n short counterexamples are equivalent (with respect to learnability) to learners using least short counterexample or just 'no', (2) learners using n least short counterexamples are strictly stronger than learners using n short arbitrary counterexamples, (3) learners using n arbitrary counterexamples are strictly weaker than learners using n least counterexamples.
